The Outlaw Trail

Robert Redford, the Wild Bunch, and 1,500 Miles of Sanctuary

Author

Ryan Lafferty

Published

March 23, 2026

The Documentary

In the summer of 1976, Robert Redford arrived in Wyoming having just finished filming All the President’s Men. He had been thinking about the Outlaw Trail for almost a decade, since the days he spent in this same country researching his role as the Sundance Kid for the 1969 film. The result was a three-week, 600-mile expedition across the length of a vanished outlaw world, documented in the November 1976 issue of National Geographic and later adapted into a 40-minute television special, The Outlaw Trail with Robert Redford, which aired in the UK on December 24, 1978.

The documentary is now rare and out of print. But the journey it captured remains one of the more honest engagements a Hollywood figure has ever made with the physical and human geography of the American West.

“I was already in love with the almost too-wild-to-be-true history of the West and Wyoming. I was fascinated by that part of the West that offered sanctuary and escape routes to hundreds of colorful, lawless men.” Robert Redford, 1976

Redford traveled with a small team that included western historian Kerry Ross Boren, National Geographic photographer Jonathan Blair, and — in one of the more improbable literary footnotes of the era — the novelist Edward Abbey, who joined the party in Moab. They traveled by horseback, car, and boat, the boat required because the Glen Canyon Dam had flooded the original route under Lake Powell thirteen years earlier.

The expedition ended in Circleville, Utah, where Redford met Lula Betenson, the elderly sister of Robert LeRoy Parker, better known as Butch Cassidy. He had first met her in 1968 during research for the film. The meeting closed a personal arc spanning eight years and gave the documentary its most resonant scene.

Redford died in September 2024 at age 88. He had founded the Sundance Institute in 1981 at his Utah ski resort, naming it after the same geography the outlaw trail runs through.

The Trail

The Outlaw Trail was not a single blazed route. It was a network: hideouts spaced roughly 200 miles apart, relay stations with fresh horses, sympathetic ranchers, and canyon systems that defeated posses as efficiently as any wall. The three main sanctuaries anchored the system. Between them ran a web of escape corridors connecting the entire mountain West.

It was active from roughly 1870 to 1910. At its peak in the late 1880s and 1890s, the network supported the most prolific train and bank robbing operation in American history. The men who used it were not romantic figures while they lived. They were pragmatic criminals who understood terrain, jurisdiction, and the economics of hospitality.

Three structural features made the trail work:

Terrain. The route threaded through canyon systems, high desert plateaus, and mountain passes that were easy to defend and nearly impossible for large posses to navigate without being spotted first.

Jurisdictional gaps. The three main hideouts sat at state and territory borders by design. A Wyoming posse had no legal standing in Utah or Colorado. A fugitive at Browns Park could step across three jurisdiction lines in an afternoon.

Sympathetic networks. Ranching families along the route supplied horses, food, and intelligence. Some from genuine goodwill, some because they had their own reasons to stay clear of law enforcement, some because the outlaws paid fairly and the alternative was worse.

Section A: Montana and Northern Wyoming

The northern end of the trail was Kid Curry country. Harvey Logan, known as the wildest man in the Wild Bunch, operated out of a horse ranch near Landusky, Montana, in Phillips County. His network of safe houses and relay points extended south through the Powder River breaks into Wyoming.

The defining location in this section is not a hideout but a jail. In August 1887, a 20-year-old Wyoming drifter named Harry Longabaugh was arrested for stealing a horse from the VVV Ranch outside Sundance, Wyoming. He served eighteen months in the Crook County jail. When he walked out in early 1889 he had a name: the Sundance Kid.

Section A: Montana & Northern Wyoming. Landusky, Malta, Sundance, Belle Fourche.

Section B: Hole-in-the-Wall Country

The Hole-in-the-Wall is not a single feature but a terrain system: a hidden valley tucked behind the Red Wall sandstone escarpment in Johnson County, Wyoming, roughly 40 miles southwest of Kaycee. A single narrow pass through the rock face opens into a bowl large enough to winter cattle and horses. At its peak the valley held cabins, corrals, and a livery stable. Posses attempting to enter did so one at a time, through a gap held by men with rifles.

The broader section holds the concentrated evidence of how the outlaw economy actually functioned. Thermopolis had the saloon network. South Pass City and Atlantic City were the ghost-town settlements where the frontier was dying in slow motion. Lander was the supply town. Wyoming Territorial Prison in Laramie was where Butch Cassidy spent two years, 1894 to 1896, for horse theft, and where he reportedly negotiated with the governor for amnesty — an offer that was eventually declined.

“My life is a dug hole.” Tex, a former San Antonio bank clerk turned Hole-in-the-Wall resident, to Robert Redford, 1976

Section B: Hole-in-the-Wall Country. Central Wyoming, Wind River Range approaches.

Section C: The Tri-Border Sanctuary Corridor

This is the operational heart of the trail: the 300-mile zone where Wyoming, Utah, and Colorado meet, threaded by the Green River canyon system. Three jurisdictions, nearly impassable terrain, and a small community of ranchers with complicated loyalties to law enforcement.

Browns Park sits at the center. A remote valley approximately 35 miles long along the Green River, straddling Moffat County, Colorado and Daggett County, Utah, with Wyoming a short ride to the north. Named for a fur trapper in the 1820s, it became the second major anchor of the outlaw network. The Bassett family ran cattle here and maintained relationships with almost every major figure in the Wild Bunch. Ann Bassett, known as the Queen of the Cattle Rustlers, was tried twice for rustling and acquitted both times. Her oral histories, collected late in her life, remain one of the primary documentary sources for the period.

John Jarvie ran a trading post on the Green River bank inside Browns Park where outlaws could buy supplies without questions. The site survives, administered by the BLM, and remains accessible by dirt road today.

Downstream, the Green River drops into the Gates of Lodore, the entrance to Dinosaur National Monument’s canyon system. Nine Mile Canyon, in Carbon and Duchesne counties, provided a transit corridor east-west across the plateau, built in 1886 by Buffalo Soldiers of the 9th Cavalry. The canyon walls hold over 10,000 rock art panels from Fremont and Ute cultures. The outlaws used the road the soldiers built.

Section C: Tri-Border Sanctuary Corridor. Browns Park, Flaming Gorge, Nine Mile Canyon.

Section D: Robbers Roost and the Canyonlands

Robbers Roost is the most extreme piece of geography on the entire trail. A roughly 2,000-square-mile maze of canyon country bounded by the Colorado River to the east, the Green River to the west, and the Dirty Devil River drainage to the north. No lawman successfully raided it during the outlaw years. The terrain made it unnecessary to defend; a posse simply could not move through it faster than someone who knew the way.

Butch Cassidy and Elzy Lay formed the Wild Bunch here in the early 1890s. The gang used it as a base of operations for the Castle Gate payroll robbery in 1897, a precisely executed daylight theft of the Pleasant Valley Coal Company payroll at the canyon mouth on the Price River. The telegraph lines were cut on the way in. The loot was never recovered.

The Castle Gate itself no longer exists. The canyon mouth was demolished in 1986 during road construction.

The section ends at Circleville, on US-89 south of town along the Sevier River, where the Parker family cabin still stands. Robert LeRoy Parker left here around age 18 and did not return with his real name. Robert Redford ended his 1976 expedition here, sitting with Lula Betenson, Butch Cassidy’s sister, at the table where her brother grew up.

Section D: Robbers Roost, Hanksville, Canyonlands, Circleville.

The Outlaws

Butch Cassidy

Robert LeRoy Parker was born in Beaver, Utah in 1866 and grew up in Circleville. His early criminal mentor was a cattle rustler named Mike Cassidy, whose surname he adopted. He was imprisoned in the Wyoming Territorial Prison in Laramie from 1894 to 1896. Upon release he attempted to negotiate amnesty with the Wyoming governor and the Union Pacific Railroad, an offer that was declined. He then organized the Wild Bunch at Robbers Roost and ran the most successful series of train and bank robberies the West had seen.

In 1901 he left for South America with the Sundance Kid and Etta Place. His official death is recorded as Bolivia, 1908, in a gunfight with the Bolivian army. Multiple witnesses in later years — including his own sister — suggested he survived and returned to the United States.

The Sundance Kid

Harry Alonzo Longabaugh was born in Phoenixville, Pennsylvania. He arrived in Wyoming in his late teens, stole a horse, and spent eighteen months in the Crook County jail in Sundance. The name he took from that town outlasted everything else he was. He was Cassidy’s most trusted partner, left for South America with him in 1901, and shares the official death date of 1908.

Kid Curry

Harvey Logan operated out of Landusky, Montana, and was by most accounts the most violent member of the Wild Bunch. He was involved in the Great Northern Train Robbery near Malta in 1901. He died in Parachute, Colorado in 1904 from a gunshot wound, likely self-inflicted to avoid capture.

Black Jack Ketchum

Thomas Ketchum worked the southern end of the trail, in New Mexico and Texas. He robbed Colorado Southern trains near Folsom, New Mexico multiple times. On his final attempt in August 1899 he went alone, was shot by the train conductor, and was captured the next day. He was tried in Clayton, New Mexico and executed on April 26, 1901. The gallows drop was miscalculated and the rope decapitated him.

Redford’s Route: 1976

Redford’s expedition covered approximately 600 miles of the southern half of the trail over three weeks. His team traveled north to south, starting at Hole-in-the-Wall and ending at the Parker cabin in Circleville. Where the original route passed under Lake Powell — flooded in 1963 by the Glen Canyon Dam — they traveled by boat.

The story Redford found was not only about the outlaws. At Hole-in-the-Wall he met ranchers losing their land to mineral rights buyers. At Atlantic City he found young back-to-the-landers in a near-unchanged gold-mining settlement. At Browns Park he collected oral histories from elderly locals who had known the Bassett family personally. At Robbers Roost he examined the Wild Bunch camp and understood, standing in it, why posses had never come.

The expedition confirmed what he had suspected in 1967: the landscape was not a backdrop to the history. It was the reason the history happened the way it did.

Notes on the Data

The waypoints in this report are drawn from historical marker databases (HMDB), BLM field station records, Utah state archives, and the National Geographic expedition account. Coordinates are approximate center points for named areas unless a specific historical marker location is documented.

No official GIS shapefile exists for the Outlaw Trail. The trail was never designated a National Historic Trail by Congress and has no authoritative NPS alignment dataset. The trail corridor shown in these maps is manually digitized from the documented waypoint sequence. It represents the approximate routing, not a surveyed or excavated path.

The BLM manages the Robbers Roost area through the Henry Mountains Field Station. Browns Park is administered as a National Wildlife Refuge by the USFWS (designated 1965). The NPS manages Dinosaur National Monument, Canyonlands National Park, and Glen Canyon NRA, all of which overlap with or abut the trail corridor.

GIS data note: An Overture Maps query of the trail corridor is pending and will be added in a future revision. This will add building footprints and current POI data for the named towns and sites.
